See the Terms and Conditions (https://onlinelibrary.wiley.com/terms-and-conditions) on Wiley Online Library for rules of use; OA articles are governed by the applicable Creative Commons License The present patients expand the spectrum of clinical features and tumor types associated with antiamphiphy- sin antibodies. There are several reports of patients with SCLC and PEM who had rigidity and spasms believed to be caused by damage or loss of spinal cord interneurons [22,23]. These patients were not tested for antineuronal antibodies. Muscle rigidity resembling stiff-man syn- drome has been observed in several patients with a variety of other neoplasms, including thymoma [24,25], Hodg- kin’s disease [ 171, and carcinomas of the breast or colon [ 171. Two patients with thymoma and paraneoplastic ri- gidity reported by Nicholas and associates [25] did not have identifiable antineuronal antibodies. Rigidity in the present patients with SCLC and antiamphiphysin anti- bodies and in the previously reported patients with breast carcinoma presumably reflects pathology in the spinal cord or brainstem or both, although direct pathological proof is lacking. Antiamphiphysin antibodies are not restricted to pa- tients with stiff-man syndrome. Two of the present pa- tients had prominent dysesthesias that began asymmet- rically and involved the face, trunk, and proximal limbs early in the course, and also had areflexia, dispropor- tionate loss of proprioception, and loss of sensory nerve action potentials. These features are typical of para- neoplastic sensory neuronopathy caused by injury to dorsal root ganglia neurons [26, 271. The pattern and severity of sensory dysfunction in Patient 1 did not differ from those of patients with sensory neuronopa- thy and ANNA-I whom I personally examined. Except for the additional presence of ANNA-1 in Patient 2, the patterns of antiamphiphysin immunore- activity by immunocytochemistry and immunoblotting were indistinguishable among the present 3 patients, despite their differing clinical presentations. Diffuse reactivity of antiamphiphysin antibodies throughout the central nervous system (CNS) is reminiscent of the panneuronal reactivity of ANNA-1 and ANNA-2 (anti-Ri antibodies) [l]. For each of these three para- neoplastic autoantibodies there is a predominant clini- cal syndrome (stiff-man syndrome, sensory neuronopa- thy, and opsoclonus/ataxia, respectively), but patients with a given autoantibody are clinically heterogeneous. To date, individual patient’s clinical features do not correlate with identifiably different patterns of immu- noreactivity of their sera with specific neuronal subsets. As with several other antineuronal autoantibodies, antiamphiphysin antibodies appear to be a useful tool for diagnosing a patient’s neurological disorder as para- neoplastic, and for indicating the probable type of underlying neoplasm [I]. The actual role of antiam- phiphysin antibodies in the pathogenesis of PEM or stiff-man syndrome is unknown. The general theory of autoimmunity for neurological paraneoplastic syn- dromes is that the immune response initially arises as an antitumor response directed against shared anti- gen(s) expressed by tumor cells and neurons [l]. Folli and colleagues [4] did not detect amphiphysin in im- munoblots of the breast tumor from one of their para- neoplastic stiff-man patients, nor from 12 breast carci- nomas from neurologically normal patients. In the present study expression of amphiphysin was more eas- ily detected by RT-PCR than by immunoblotting. It is not known whether this is due to the greater sensitiv- ity of RT-PCR or to differences in immunoreactivity of amphiphysin expressed by neurons versus tumor cells. The RT-PCR results also suggest the possibility of alternate splicing of amphiphysin RNA in tumors; this is presently under further study. Expression of the amphiphysin gene in some SCLCs and breast carcino- mas indirectly supports the general theory of auto- immunity in paraneoplastic disorders, but does not provide insight into the mechanism(s) of immune- mediated neuronal injury. Three of the 5 reported patients with breast cancer, stiff-man syndrome, and antiamphiphysin antibodies had neurological improvement with prednisone and tu- mor resection [4, 161. Of the 3 patients reported in detail by Folli and colleagues [4], one became “neuro- logically normal” and one regained independent ambu- lation. The third patient was not treated with steroids and had progressive rigidity despite treatment by tumor resection, diazepam, and baclofen [4]. Patient 3 in the present report partially improved with chemotherapy and immunotherapy, but still could not walk. The other 2 present patients did not improve despite che- motherapy, corticosteroids, and intravenous immuno- globulin (and a fall in antiamphiphysin antibody ti- ters). Their clinical course was more typical of PEM and SCLC [I, 21, namely, either a pattern of subacute deterioration and subsequent leveling off at severe neu- rological disability (Patient I), or progressive neurolog- ical deterioration despite aggressive treatment (Patient 2). The small number of reported patients with anti- amphiphysin antibodies does not allow any firm state- ments as to whether patients with breast carcinoma have a better neurological outcome than do patients with SCLC. Until more data become available, it seems reasonable to treat patients with paraneoplastic disor- ders and antiamphiphysin antibodies with a combina- tion of antitumor treatment, corticosteroids, and possi- bly intravenous immunoglobulin.
